The geometry of gravity · exact solutions of Einstein's field equations

Black Holes

A region where matter has bent spacetime so steeply that not even light moves fast enough to leave. Below: the exact geometries general relativity predicts — Schwarzschild, Reissner–Nordström, Kerr — worked out, drawn, and connected to what telescopes now see.

A black hole, ray-traced from the Schwarzschild metric — light bent into a ring, the disk lifted over the shadow, one side beamed brighter.

00 · what a black hole is

An escape velocity that outruns light

Pile enough mass into a small enough volume and the speed you would need to escape its gravity climbs past the speed of light. Since nothing outpaces light, nothing gets out — you have a black hole.

The idea is older than relativity. In 1783 John Michell imagined a star so massive that light could not escape it; Laplace repeated the thought a few years later. But Newtonian gravity was the wrong language. The right one arrived in 1915, when Einstein's general relativity recast gravity not as a force but as the curvature of spacetime: mass and energy tell spacetime how to bend, and that bending tells matter and light how to move.

A black hole is the most extreme expression of that idea. Its defining feature is the event horizon — a one-way surface. Cross it and every future-pointing path leads inward; leaving would mean moving backward in time. The horizon hides a singularity, a place where the curvature the theory predicts grows without bound and general relativity itself stops making sense. The term "black hole" was popularized by John Wheeler in 1967; the first photograph of one came in 2019.

Remarkably, the geometry of a settled black hole is simple. A theorem — informally, "black holes have no hair" — says that once a black hole stops ringing, everything about it is captured by just three numbers: its mass, its electric charge, and its spin. That is the whole reason this page has the shape it does. Each exact solution below switches those knobs on one at a time.

The rules: Einstein's field equations

General relativity is encoded in ten coupled, nonlinear differential equations relating the geometry of spacetime (the left side) to its matter–energy content (the right side):

Einstein field equations — geometry ⟷ matter
\[ G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda\,g_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}\,T_{\mu\nu} \]
\(g_{\mu\nu}\) is the metric — the object that measures distances and times. \(G_{\mu\nu}\) packages its curvature; \(T_{\mu\nu}\) is the energy and momentum of matter; \(\Lambda\) is the cosmological constant. In empty space around an isolated mass, \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\) and \(\Lambda\) is negligible, leaving the vacuum equations \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\).

"Solving" for a black hole means finding the metric \(g_{\mu\nu}\) — equivalently the line element \(ds^2\), the recipe for the spacetime interval between neighboring events — that satisfies these equations with the right symmetry. Do that with mass only, and you get Schwarzschild. Add charge: Reissner–Nordström. Add spin: Kerr. Add both: Kerr–Newman. The rest of this page is those four solutions, in order.

A note on units

Formulas below keep \(G\) and \(c\) explicit, but figures often use geometric units where \(G=c=1\) and lengths are measured in units of \(M\). In those units the horizon sits at \(r_s=2M\), the photon sphere at \(3M\), and the innermost stable orbit at \(6M\). Multiply by \(GM/c^2\) to get meters.

01 · mass only · 1916 · Karl Schwarzschild

The Schwarzschild solution

The first and simplest exact black hole: no charge, no spin, perfectly spherical. Schwarzschild found it within months of Einstein's theory — while serving on the Russian front, months before he died of illness.

Schwarzschild metric — vacuum, static, spherically symmetric
\[ ds^{2}=-\Bigl(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\Bigr)c^{2}dt^{2}+\Bigl(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\Bigr)^{-1}dr^{2}+r^{2}\,d\Omega^{2} \]
r_s = 2GM/c²  —  the Schwarzschild radius (event horizon)
dΩ² = dθ² + sin²θ dφ²  —  the two-sphere of angles

Where does it come from? Assume the spacetime is static (unchanging, no rotation) and spherically symmetric. The most general such metric is \(ds^2=-A(r)c^2dt^2+B(r)dr^2+r^2d\Omega^2\). Feed this into the vacuum equations \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\); the equations force \(A(r)=1/B(r)=1-r_s/r\), with the constant \(r_s\) fixed by matching Newton's law far away. A bonus falls out — Birkhoff's theorem: any spherically symmetric vacuum is exactly this, even if the source pulsates. A spherically breathing star radiates no gravitational waves, and the field outside is static regardless.

Two very different singularities

The metric misbehaves in two places. At \(r=r_s\) the \(dt^2\) term vanishes and the \(dr^2\) term blows up — but this is only a coordinate artifact, like the way longitude lines crowd at the North Pole. Switch to better coordinates and spacetime is perfectly smooth there. The horizon is a real surface, but nothing infinite happens to a falling observer as they cross it.

At \(r=0\) the story is different. A coordinate-independent measure of curvature, the Kretschmann scalar \(R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=48G^2M^2/c^4 r^6\), genuinely diverges. That is a true singularity — a breakdown of the theory, widely believed to be a signal that quantum gravity must take over.

The shadow and the photon sphere

Light bends near mass, and near a black hole it bends catastrophically. A photon aimed with an impact parameter smaller than \(b_c=3\sqrt{3}\,GM/c^2\approx 5.2\,r_s/2\) spirals through the horizon and is lost; a photon just outside that value whips around and escapes. The boundary between capture and escape is what makes a black hole cast a dark shadow on any bright background — the feature the Event Horizon Telescope resolved.

Time itself slows down

The factor \(\sqrt{1-r_s/r}\) multiplying \(dt\) is gravitational time dilation. A clock at radius \(r\) ticks slower than one far away by exactly this factor; light climbing out is redshifted by it. At the horizon the factor reaches zero: to a distant observer, an infalling clock appears to freeze and fade to red, never quite crossing. The faller, meanwhile, sails through in finite time and notices nothing locally special.

Inside the horizon

Cross \(r_s\) and the roles of \(r\) and \(t\) swap: the radial direction becomes time-like. Decreasing \(r\) is now as unavoidable as moving into the future. The singularity is not a place ahead of you in space — it is a moment in your future. No rocket, however powerful, can steer around a time.

02 · mass + charge · 1916–1918 · Reissner, Weyl, Nordström

Reissner–Nordström: adding charge

Give the black hole an electric charge and it stops being empty — its own electromagnetic field now curves spacetime too. Found almost immediately after Schwarzschild, it splits the single horizon into two.

Reissner–Nordström metric — electrovacuum (Einstein–Maxwell)
\[ ds^{2}=-f(r)\,c^{2}dt^{2}+\frac{dr^{2}}{f(r)}+r^{2}\,d\Omega^{2},\qquad f(r)=1-\frac{r_s}{r}+\frac{r_Q^{2}}{r^{2}} \]
r_Q² = G Q² / (4π ε₀ c⁴)  —  a length set by the charge Q
r_± = ½ r_s ± √( ¼ r_s² − r_Q² )  —  the two horizons

Charge means the vacuum equations no longer apply: the electromagnetic field carries energy, so \(T_{\mu\nu}\neq 0\). One solves the coupled Einstein–Maxwell system instead. The result adds a single \(+r_Q^2/r^2\) term to the metric function — but that term changes the horizon structure completely, because it lets \(f(r)\) have two roots.

Three regimes

Reading off the horizons \(r_\pm=\tfrac{1}{2}r_s\pm\sqrt{\tfrac14 r_s^2-r_Q^2}\):

Q < M
two horizons

An outer event horizon \(r_+\) and an inner Cauchy horizon \(r_-\). Between them, as in Schwarzschild, you must fall inward; but past \(r_-\) you can move freely again and even avoid the singularity.

Q = M
extremal

The two horizons merge into one at \(r=M\). Extremal black holes have exactly zero Hawking temperature and play a starring role in string-theory counts of black-hole entropy.

Q > M
naked

No horizon at all — the singularity would be visible to the outside universe. Penrose's cosmic censorship conjecture proposes nature forbids this. Nothing known lets you overcharge a hole past \(Q=M\).

Why real black holes aren't charged

The universe is full of free charges. A charged black hole preferentially attracts the opposite sign and repels its own, neutralizing in a heartbeat. So Reissner–Nordström is mostly a theorist's black hole — but an indispensable one: it introduced the inner horizon, the extremal limit, and the specter of naked singularities, all of which reappear in the spinning case that does describe reality.

03 · mass + spin · 1963 · Roy Kerr

Kerr: the spinning black hole

Every real black hole rotates, so this is the one nature actually uses. It took 47 years after Schwarzschild to find — the equations lose their spherical symmetry, and the answer is far from obvious.

Kerr metric — Boyer–Lindquist coordinates
\[ ds^{2}=-\Bigl(1-\frac{r_s r}{\Sigma}\Bigr)c^{2}dt^{2}-\frac{2\,r_s r\,a\,c\sin^{2}\theta}{\Sigma}\,dt\,d\varphi+\frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}dr^{2}+\Sigma\,d\theta^{2}+\Bigl(r^{2}+a^{2}+\frac{r_s r\,a^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{\Sigma}\Bigr)\sin^{2}\theta\,d\varphi^{2} \]
Σ = r² + a² cos²θ   |   Δ = r² − r_s r + a²   |   a = J / (M c)   — the spin per unit mass
r_± = ½ r_s ± √( ¼ r_s² − a² )   —   horizons   |   extremal when a = M

The tell-tale new piece is the cross term \(dt\,d\varphi\): time and angle are now mixed. Physically, the black hole's rotation drags spacetime around with it. This is frame dragging (the Lense–Thirring effect), and it has a dramatic consequence.

The ergosphere: where you cannot stand still

Outside the horizon lies a second surface, the static limit. Between it and the horizon is the ergosphere. Inside it, frame dragging is so strong that no observer can remain at rest relative to the distant stars — you are forced to co-rotate, no matter how hard you fire your engines. Yet you can still escape outward, because you are outside the true horizon.

The ergosphere is not just a curiosity. Because it lies outside the horizon, energy can be extracted from it: drop an object in, let it split so one piece falls through the horizon on a negative-energy orbit, and the escaping piece carries out more energy than you put in — mined from the hole's rotation. This is the Penrose process, and its wave analogue, superradiance, may power the enormous jets astronomers see blasting from galactic centers.

Spin reshapes the orbits

How fast a black hole spins changes where matter can orbit. For co-rotating (prograde) orbits, the innermost stable circular orbit shrinks from \(6M\) at zero spin all the way down to \(M\) for a maximal hole; counter-rotating orbits get pushed out to \(9M\). Because the inner edge of an accretion disk sits at that orbit, faster spin lets gas orbit deeper in a stronger field — and radiate far more efficiently before it falls in.

How efficient is a black hole?

The energy released as matter spirals from far away to the innermost stable orbit is pure gravitational binding energy turned to light. For a non-spinning hole that is about 5.7% of the rest-mass energy \(mc^2\); for a maximally spinning Kerr hole it reaches roughly 42%. Compare nuclear fusion in the Sun at ~0.7%. Accreting black holes are the most efficient steady engines in the universe.

04 · mass + charge + spin · 1965 · Ezra Newman

Kerr–Newman: the whole family

Turn on all three knobs at once and you get the most general stationary black hole. Every solution above is a special case — set spin to zero for Reissner–Nordström, charge to zero for Kerr, both to zero for Schwarzschild.

The Kerr–Newman metric has the same form as Kerr, with a single change absorbing the charge into the horizon function:

Kerr–Newman — the master electrovacuum solution
\[ \Delta = r^{2}-r_s\,r+a^{2}+r_Q^{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r_\pm=\tfrac12 r_s\pm\sqrt{\tfrac14 r_s^{2}-a^{2}-r_Q^{2}} \]
Everything else — \(\Sigma\), the cross term, the ergosphere — carries over from Kerr. A horizon exists only while \(a^2+r_Q^2\le\tfrac14 r_s^2\), i.e. \(M^2\ge a^2+Q^2\). Push past it and, again, you would expose a naked singularity.

This is the mathematical statement of no hair. The full theorem: any stationary, asymptotically flat, electrovacuum black hole is a Kerr–Newman black hole, fixed entirely by mass \(M\), charge \(Q\), and angular momentum \(J\). Two black holes with the same three numbers are identical — no memory of the star, gas, or spaceships that made them. It is hard to overstate how strange this is: a black hole is macroscopically simpler than a hydrogen atom.

Since real black holes shed charge almost instantly, astrophysics runs on the \(Q=0\) slice: every observed black hole is, to superb accuracy, a Kerr black hole. Kerr–Newman remains the elegant capstone that unifies the family.

What black holes actually do

The metrics are the skeleton. Hang real physics on them — hot gas, quantum fields, gravitational waves — and black holes become some of the loudest, brightest, strangest objects in the sky.

They shine by accretion

Black holes themselves emit nothing, but the gas they capture does. Infalling matter forms a flattened, differentially rotating accretion disk; friction and magnetic stress heat it to millions of degrees until it blazes in X-rays. Twisted magnetic fields can launch relativistic jets from the poles, spanning thousands of light-years. The disk in the hero image at the top shows two hallmarks the Kerr geometry predicts: the near side lensed up and over the shadow, and one edge beamed brighter because that gas is rushing toward us at a fair fraction of light speed.

They aren't perfectly black — Hawking radiation

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that quantum effects at the horizon make a black hole glow with a faint thermal spectrum at temperature

Hawking temperature  ·  and Bekenstein–Hawking entropy
\[ T_{H}=\frac{\hbar c^{3}}{8\pi G M k_{B}} \qquad\qquad S_{BH}=\frac{k_{B}\,c^{3}A}{4 G\hbar},\quad A=4\pi r_s^{2} \]
The temperature is inversely proportional to mass: small holes are hot, giant ones are colder than deep space. The entropy scales with horizon area, not volume — a clue that gravity may be fundamentally holographic.

The consequences are profound. A black hole slowly radiates its mass away and eventually evaporates; a solar-mass hole would take about \(10^{67}\) years, far longer than the age of the universe, while a tiny primordial one could be exploding now. Evaporation also creates the information paradox: if a hole is fully described by \(M\), \(Q\), \(J\) and then vanishes into featureless thermal radiation, what happened to the information that fell in? Reconciling this is a central goal of quantum gravity.

They collide, and spacetime rings

When two black holes spiral together and merge, they radiate a burst of gravitational waves — ripples in spacetime itself. The signal sweeps up in frequency and amplitude (the inspiral), peaks at the merger, then fades as the new hole settles (the ringdown). LIGO caught the first, GW150914, in September 2015.

Near a small hole your feet fall faster than your head; the difference stretches you thin. Near a supermassive one, the tide at the horizon is gentle.

Because the horizon grows with mass, the biggest black holes enclose an average density lower than air. Size, not compactness, defines them.

observation · the evidence

Seeing the invisible

For a century black holes were pure theory. In the last decade they became data — imaged, weighed, and heard as they collide.

Heard as well as seen

Gravitational-wave detectors add an entirely independent line of evidence. Since the 2015 debut, the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network has confirmed roughly 390 events — mostly merging black holes — with its fourth observing run wrapping up in November 2025. One 2025 signal, GW250114, was recorded so cleanly that it delivered the most precise test of general relativity yet and directly confirmed Hawking's theorem that a black hole's horizon area can never decrease.

Add the decades of infrared orbits tracing stars whipping around the invisible mass at the Galactic center — work that earned the 2020 Nobel Prize alongside Roger Penrose's black-hole theorems — and the case is overwhelming. The geometries on this page are not just elegant mathematics. They are what is out there.

What's next

The next-generation Event Horizon Telescope and the proposed space-based Black Hole Explorer aim to resolve the razor-thin photon ring — the stack of images from light that loops the hole multiple times before escaping. Its precise shape is a near-pure prediction of the Kerr metric, and measuring it would be a direct, high-precision test of Einstein's gravity in the strongest fields we can reach.
